Revelation 3:10-11: to Philadelphia Jesus says "I am coming soon", in a letter to a real first-century city.
John 14:23: Jesus and the Father will "come" and make their home with the one who loves him.

Many scholars of all views agree the church warnings are historical visits in judgment. Some, like Robert Thomas, argue they are threats tied to the final coming, which would affect those churches if it came in their time. Others see both: near judgments that preview the final one.
What did Jesus mean when he said some standing there would not taste death before seeing him come in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28)?
On this reading, he meant a coming within their lifetime: the judgment on Jerusalem and the full showing of his kingdom. Some disciples, such as John, lived to see it.

Jesus said the Son of Man would come with his angels in his Father's glory and repay each person. Then he added: "Some standing here will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom" (Matthew 16:27-28). "Not taste death" implies that most would die but some would still be alive. That fits a span of about forty years, not a week. Henry Alford tied this to the destruction of Jerusalem and the clear display of Christ's kingdom. Peter later asked about John, and Jesus said, "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" (John 21:22). On this reading, the question about "the end of the age" was asked with this promise in mind.
Matthew 10:23: "You will not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes."
Early tradition says John lived into the reign of Trajan, around AD 98 (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5; 3.3.4).

Many interpreters link Matthew 16:28 to the transfiguration six days later (Matthew 17:1-8), as 2 Peter 1:16-18 seems to do. Others point to the resurrection or Pentecost. Some see AD 70. Futurists usually choose the transfiguration as a preview of the second coming.
To whom did Jesus say, "See that no one leads you astray" (Matthew 24:4)?
To the disciples sitting with him on the Mount of Olives. This reading says the warning was first for them and the events they would face.

The discourse was given in private to Peter, James, John and Andrew (Mark 13:3). Jesus said to them: "See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray" (Matthew 24:4-5). He told them they would hear of wars and must not be alarmed. He said, "They will deliver you up... and kill you, and you will be hated" (Matthew 24:9). On the fulfilled reading, the conclusion is direct. The warnings were for the generation that asked about the temple. Comparing the New Testament with historians of the time shows the predicted signs happening before the Roman attack on Jerusalem. That does not make the passage useless for us. It teaches us how faithful Jesus' words are and how to stand firm under deception.
Mark 13:3 names the four listeners: Peter, James, John and Andrew.
Acts 20:29-30: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in and men would rise to draw disciples away.

Futurists say the disciples represent believers, or the Jewish remnant, at the end of history. Many amillennial and historic premillennial readers see the warnings as for all believers in every age, with AD 70 as the first case. Christians of all views use the passage as a call to discernment today.
Did false messiahs and false prophets appear before AD 70?
Yes. Acts and Josephus name several leaders who drew crowds with promises of deliverance, especially in the 40s and 50s AD.

Gamaliel mentioned Theudas, who claimed to be somebody, and Judas the Galilean, who led a revolt at the census (Acts 5:36-37). Josephus describes a Theudas under the governor Fadus (about AD 45) who said he was a prophet and would part the Jordan. Roman cavalry killed many and beheaded him (Antiquities 20.5.1). Under Felix (AD 52-59) an Egyptian false prophet led thousands to the Mount of Olives, promising Jerusalem's walls would fall (Antiquities 20.8.6; Acts 21:38). Josephus says impostors and deceivers persuaded crowds into the desert with promised signs, and many were killed (Jewish War 2.13.4). On the fulfilled reading, this is exactly what Jesus foretold. Strictly, Jesus warned of both false christs and false prophets (Matthew 24:24), and these men fit one or both labels.
Acts 21:38: the Roman officer asked Paul, "Are you not the Egyptian who led four thousand men into the wilderness?"
Josephus (Jewish War 6.5.2) says a false prophet led people to the temple during the fire of AD 70, promising signs of deliverance; about six thousand died.

Many scholars note that Gamaliel's Theudas (spoken of about AD 35) seems earlier than Josephus' Theudas (about AD 45); there may have been two men of that name. Futurists agree false leaders arose then but expect a final wave of deception led by the Antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:9-10).
What do early sources say about Simon the magician of Acts 8?
Acts says he claimed to be "someone great" and was called "the Great Power of God". Second-century writers say he claimed divine status and gained followers in Rome.

Luke records that Simon practised magic in Samaria and amazed the people. They said, "This man is the power of God that is called Great" (Acts 8:9-10). Justin Martyr, himself from Samaria, wrote around AD 155 that Simon came to Rome under Claudius and was honored as a god (First Apology 26). Irenaeus said Simon presented himself as a high divine power (Against Heresies 1.23). On the fulfilled reading, Simon is an early example of someone "saying, I am he". One correction is needed. Justin said a statue in Rome was inscribed "To Simon the holy god". In 1574 a base was found on the Tiber island reading "Semoni Sanco Deo Fidio". It honored Semo Sancus, a Sabine god. Justin probably misread it. Simon's claims are still well attested.
Acts 8:18-24: Simon tried to buy the power to give the Spirit; from his name comes the word "simony".
Eusebius (Church History 2.13) repeats Justin's account and calls Simon the first author of heresy.

Scholars of all views treat the later Simon stories with caution, since they grew over time. Most agree he was a real figure who made great claims. Some see him less as a messiah figure and more as an early Gnostic teacher, which fits Jesus' warning about false prophets rather than false christs.
Are false messiahs in our day a fulfillment of Matthew 24:5?
Not on this reading. False christs still appear, and believers must reject them. But the prophecy was fulfilled in the generation before AD 70.

Since the first century many people have claimed to be Christ or a messiah. Examples include Simon bar Kokhba (AD 132), Sabbatai Zevi (1665) and many modern cult leaders. Christians must test every spirit, because many false prophets have gone out into the world (1 John 4:1). On the fulfilled reading, however, the presence of false christs today does not fulfill Matthew 24:5. Jesus set the time limit of "this generation" (Matthew 24:34). The deceivers he predicted came in that period. Later deceivers repeat the pattern but are not the sign Jesus gave. This distinction matters. It keeps believers from reading each new cult leader as a countdown signal, and it keeps the focus on the clear warning: do not follow anyone but the true Christ.
Simon bar Kokhba led the revolt of AD 132-135; Rabbi Akiva hailed him as messiah. It ended in disaster for Judea.
1 John 2:18 says "many antichrists have come; therefore we know that it is the last hour": John saw them in his own day.

Futurists teach that false christs will increase toward the end and climax in the Antichrist. Many amillennial readers see Matthew 24:5 as a pattern for the whole church age, fulfilled again and again. Both agree that false messiahs today must be resisted with Scripture.
Is our generation seeing signs that no earlier generation has seen?
This reading says no. War, famine, plague and earthquake fill all of history. Jesus tied his signs to the generation of his hearers.

Many modern books claim that no previous generation has seen so many signs so close together. But the history of the world is full of war, famine and disease. The fourteenth century lost perhaps a third of Europe to the Black Death. The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) devastated central Europe. Every age has had reasons to think the end was near. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus gave a clear time frame for his signs: "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place" (Matthew 24:34). The signs were meant to warn the disciples to flee before Jerusalem fell (Luke 21:20-21). History shows those signs did appear between about AD 30 and 70. Reading them into our news overlooks both the time text and the record of history.
The Antonine Plague (AD 165-180) killed millions across the Roman Empire, long after AD 70.
The influenza pandemic of 1918 killed tens of millions; many at the time saw it as an end-time sign.

Futurists answer that the signs are like birth pains: they grow in frequency and strength toward the end (Matthew 24:8). They point to world wars, nuclear weapons and global reach as new. Amillennial readers say the signs mark the whole age and call every generation to be ready.
How could there be "wars and rumors of wars" during the Roman Peace?
The Roman Peace was fragile. Revolts, border wars and riots broke out across the empire, and Jesus' warning stood out because people expected peace.

Augustus began the Pax Romana after the civil wars ended (about 27 BC). Rome boasted of peace. But peace was never complete. In AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple. Jews refused, and war seemed certain until his death in AD 41 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.8.2-9). Tacitus in his Annals reports troubles in Germany, Africa, Thrace, Gaul, Britain and Armenia. Boudica's revolt in Britain (AD 60-61) killed tens of thousands. On the fulfilled reading, "wars and rumors of wars" make a fitting sign in a time that boasted of peace. Jesus told his disciples not to be alarmed: "the end is not yet" (Matthew 24:6). These events were the first birth pains, not the final blow.
The near-war over Caligula's statue (AD 40-41) was a "rumor of war" that came to the very temple.
Tacitus, Histories 1.2, describes the period AD 69 as "rich in disasters, terrible with battles, torn by civil strife".

Futurists note that wars have always existed and so cannot alone be a final sign. They argue that Jesus' point was that wars are not the end, and the real signs are those later in the discourse. Many readers of all views see the verse as a warning against panic in any age.
What conflicts in the first century fit "nation will rise against nation"?
Riots and massacres between Jews and Greeks or Syrians in many cities, the Jewish revolt, and Rome's own civil wars all happened before AD 70.

Josephus records that when the war began in AD 66, the Greeks of Caesarea killed about twenty thousand Jews in one hour (Jewish War 2.18.1). Fighting then spread through the cities of Syria, where Jews and Gentiles divided into armed camps. In Alexandria about fifty thousand Jews died (Jewish War 2.18.8). In Damascus about ten thousand were killed (Jewish War 2.20.2). Earlier, around AD 40, more than fifty thousand Jews were killed at Seleucia in Mesopotamia (Antiquities 18.9.9). On the fulfilled reading, these clashes between peoples ("nation against nation") and between realms ("kingdom against kingdom") fit Jesus' words in time and place. They show that the birth pains were real and intense for the generation he addressed. The suffering fell heavily on Jewish communities, and that should be remembered with sorrow.
Jewish War 2.18.2: after Caesarea, Josephus says every city in Syria was divided into two armies.
Josephus says he gave only a brief account of Rome's civil wars because so many other writers had described them (Jewish War 4.9.2).

Futurists read "nation against nation" as a global pattern of wars at the end, often linking it to the world wars of the twentieth century. Some scholars note the phrase echoes Isaiah 19:2 and 2 Chronicles 15:6, where it describes local chaos in judgment, which suits either a first-century or a later setting.
What was the "year of the four emperors", and why does it matter here?
In AD 68-69 four men held power in Rome in quick succession: Nero, Galba, Otho and Vitellius. All died violently, showing how unstable the empire was before Jerusalem fell.

Nero killed himself in June AD 68. Galba was murdered in January 69. Otho took his own life in April 69. Vitellius was killed in December 69 as Vespasian's forces took Rome. Vespasian had been leading the war in Judea. He left his son Titus to finish the siege of Jerusalem, which fell in AD 70. On the fulfilled reading, this crisis fits Jesus' picture of kingdoms in turmoil. It also shows how closely the Jewish war was tied to the empire's fate. Some even see a link with Revelation 17:10, which speaks of seven kings, "five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come". On a Neronic dating, the sixth king would be Nero, and the brief seventh would be Galba.
Tacitus (Histories 1.4) says the death of Nero revealed a secret of empire: an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome.
Suetonius (Vespasian 4-5) reports a widespread belief that men from Judea would rule the world; Vespasian was proclaimed emperor in the east in July 69.

Historians accept these facts. The debate is about their prophetic meaning. Futurists see Revelation 17 as describing future kingdoms or empires. Scholars who date Revelation to about AD 95 read the seven kings differently. Many simply treat the year of four emperors as background, not fulfillment.
Was there a famine in the first century that fits Jesus' words?
Yes. The prophet Agabus foretold a great famine over the world, and Luke says it happened under Claudius (AD 41-54). Roman writers also record food shortages then.

Acts records that Agabus, speaking by the Spirit, predicted "a great famine over all the world" (oikoumene). Luke adds, "This took place in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28). The believers in Antioch sent relief to Judea. Later Paul collected gifts from churches in Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia for the poor in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1-3; Romans 15:25-26). Josephus describes severe famine in Judea about AD 46-48, when Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain from Egypt for the city (Antiquities 20.2.5). Tacitus says that in AD 51 Rome had only fifteen days of grain left (Annals 12.43). On the fulfilled reading, the disciples hearing these reports would have remembered Jesus' words on the Mount of Olives.
Suetonius (Claudius 18) says Claudius was pelted with crusts in the Forum during a grain shortage.
Acts 11:29-30: each disciple gave as able, and Barnabas and Saul carried the gift to the elders in Judea.

Futurists agree famines occurred then but argue they were local and limited. They expect worldwide famine in the future tribulation (Revelation 6:5-8). Many scholars note that famines happen in every age, so Jesus listed them as "the beginning of birth pains" rather than as a precise end-time clock.
How severe was the famine during the siege of Jerusalem?
Extremely severe. Josephus describes houses full of the dying and streets full of the dead as Titus' siege cut off all food.

In AD 70 Titus surrounded Jerusalem with a wall to stop people leaving and food entering (Jewish War 5.12.1-2). This fulfilled Jesus' words that enemies would "set up a barricade around you and surround you" (Luke 19:43). Josephus writes that famine then swallowed whole houses and families. Upper rooms were full of dying women and children, and lanes were full of the old who had died. Young men wandered the markets like shadows, swollen from hunger, and fell where they stood (Jewish War 5.12.3). He even records the terrible case of a mother named Mary who ate her child (Jewish War 6.3.4). On the fulfilled reading, war and famine go together, and Jesus lists famines right after wars. His tears over the city (Luke 19:41) show this was a grief to him, not a triumph.
Deuteronomy 28:53-57 warned that in a siege parents would eat their children. Lamentations 4:10 records this in 586 BC.
Luke 23:28-29: Jesus told the women of Jerusalem to weep for themselves and their children.

Most Christian readers accept that the siege fulfilled Luke 19:43-44 and Luke 21:20-24. Futurists separate these Luke texts, which they agree describe AD 70, from Matthew 24:15-22, which they see as a future great tribulation. Some scholars caution that Josephus may have heightened some details for effect.
Did Jesus say earthquakes would increase in number and strength before the end?
No. He said there would be earthquakes "in various places" and Luke says "great earthquakes". He said nothing about a rising count.

Some modern writers claim the Lord meant earthquakes of record-breaking size and number. But Jesus simply said, "There will be famines and earthquakes in various places" (Matthew 24:7). Luke adds "great earthquakes" (Luke 21:11). He does not say they will grow in frequency. Geologists also report that the number of strong earthquakes has stayed fairly steady. The apparent rise is because there are far more seismic stations to record small quakes. Christian geologist Steven Austin and New Testament scholar Mark Strauss made this point in 1999. On the fulfilled reading, the claim of an "increase" is read into the text. It also sets believers up for disappointment, since the data do not show it. The sign was met in the generation Jesus addressed.
The United States Geological Survey reports that large quakes (magnitude 7 or more) average about 15 a year, with no long-term rise.
In 1931 there were about 350 seismic stations worldwide; today there are thousands, so many more small quakes are recorded.

Some futurists still argue that the birth-pain image implies increasing intensity. Others agree there is no statistical increase and say earthquakes are simply among the signs that mark the age. Many scholars see earthquakes in prophecy as symbols of God shaking the nations (Haggai 2:6).
Were there significant earthquakes before AD 70?
Yes. The Bible records earthquakes at the cross, the resurrection and in Philippi. Roman writers record quakes at Laodicea, Pompeii and many other places.

Matthew records an earthquake when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51-54) and a great earthquake at the resurrection (Matthew 28:2). Acts tells of a great earthquake that shook the prison in Philippi (Acts 16:26). Outside the Bible, Tacitus says Laodicea was ruined by an earthquake in AD 60 and rebuilt without Roman help (Annals 14.27). A strong quake damaged Pompeii in February AD 62 (Tacitus, Annals 15.22; Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1). Some writers date it to 63. Crete, Smyrna, Chios, Samos, Hierapolis, Colossae and Rome are also listed in this period. Josephus records a violent storm and earthquake in Judea in AD 68, which he said showed God's anger (Jewish War 4.4.5). On the fulfilled reading, the sign was met in full in that generation.
Revelation 3:17 has the church at Laodicea saying "I am rich", and Tacitus confirms the city rebuilt itself from its own wealth.
Edward Plumptre wrote that perhaps no period was so marked by such shocks as the years between the cross and the fall of Jerusalem.

Few dispute these events. Futurists respond that first-century quakes were a foretaste, and that the final period will include a greater quake than any before (Revelation 16:18). Some readers see Jesus' list as general marks of the whole age, so quakes in any era are reminders, not timers.
Were there "terrors and great signs from heaven" (Luke 21:11) before AD 70?
Yes. Roman and Jewish writers record comets and strange sights in the sky in those years, including a comet that stood over Jerusalem.

Luke alone records "terrors and great signs from heaven" in his list of wars, quakes, famines and plagues. In the ancient world comets were often seen as signs of political change. Tacitus says a comet appeared in AD 60, and people began to ask who would succeed Nero (Annals 14.22). Suetonius says that after a comet Nero put to death leading men and their families (Nero 36). Halley's Comet passed in AD 66, the year the Jewish war began. Josephus writes of "a star resembling a sword" over the city and a comet that lasted a whole year (Jewish War 6.5.3). He also describes a bright light around the altar at night and a heavy temple gate opening by itself. On the fulfilled reading, Luke 21:11 was met within the generation.
Tacitus (Histories 5.13) records that armies were seen clashing in the sky and the temple doors opened, with a voice saying the gods were leaving.
Matthew 2:1-3: a star brought joy to the wise men but alarm to Herod, who feared a rival.

Futurists say these sights were minor compared with the cosmic signs still to come (Revelation 6:12-14). Skeptical historians treat the portents as legends that grew after the event. Some interpreters read "signs from heaven" symbolically, as God's judgments on rulers, rather than as astronomy.
Must the heavenly signs of Luke 21:11 have a modern, sensational fulfillment?
This reading says no. When a first-century fulfillment is on record, stretching the text to fit UFOs or modern technology misreads it.

Some popular writers, such as Chuck Missler, have suggested that Luke 21:11 points to UFOs or alien and demonic activity in our time. The fulfilled reading answers that this stretches Jesus' words beyond their plain meaning. Jesus gave these signs to his disciples so they would know when to flee Jerusalem (Luke 21:20-21). A sign is useful only to the people who are meant to see it. The first-century record shows comets, portents and fear in exactly that period. To skip over that record and search for a modern match puts speculation in place of history. It also makes the Bible's message depend on the latest trend. The safer method is to ask what the first hearers would have understood.
Luke 21:28: "When these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads." The signs were for those who would live through them.
Deuteronomy 29:29: secret things belong to the Lord, but revealed things belong to us and our children.

Most scholars of all views reject UFO readings. Futurists who do not hold such ideas still expect literal cosmic disturbances in the future. Amillennial readers often see the heavenly signs as symbols that recur whenever God judges proud powers.
Were the disciples delivered up to tribulation and killed, as Matthew 24:9 says?
Yes. Acts records arrests, floggings and the deaths of Stephen and James. Peter and Paul were killed under Nero, before AD 70.

Persecution began soon after Pentecost. Peter and John were jailed and warned (Acts 4:3, 17). They were later flogged (Acts 5:40). Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:54-60). A great persecution scattered the church from Jerusalem (Acts 8:1). Herod Agrippa I killed James the brother of John with the sword and arrested Peter (Acts 12:1-3). Paul was stoned at Lystra and left for dead (Acts 14:19). He lists beatings, lashes and dangers from both Jews and Gentiles (2 Corinthians 11:24-26). He stood before Gallio, Felix, Festus and Agrippa (Acts 18:12; 24-26). Tacitus says Nero blamed Christians for the fire of AD 64 and had them killed in cruel ways (Annals 15.44). Early tradition says Peter and Paul died in that persecution (1 Clement 5). On the fulfilled reading, Matthew 24:9 came true in detail.
Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Christians were covered with animal skins and torn by dogs, or set on fire as torches at night.
Revelation 1:9: John calls himself a "partner in the tribulation" with the churches.

Futurists agree persecution happened then but see Matthew 24:9 as also describing a future tribulation for believers, especially Jewish believers, under the Antichrist. Many amillennial readers see the verse as true of the whole church age. No view denies the first-century persecutions.
Were Christians "hated by all nations" before AD 70?
In a real sense, yes. They faced hostility from Jewish authorities in Judea and from pagan crowds and rulers across the empire, climaxing in Nero's persecution.

Jesus said, "You will be hated by all nations for my name's sake" (Matthew 24:9). In Acts, believers are opposed in Jerusalem, Damascus, Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus. They are called men who "have turned the world upside down" (Acts 17:6). Jews in Rome told Paul that this sect was "spoken against everywhere" (Acts 28:22). Tacitus calls Christians a group hated for their "crimes" and charged with "hatred of the human race" (Annals 15.44). Tertullian later wrote that the very name of Christian was under attack (Apology 2). On the fulfilled reading, this widespread hatred within Jesus' generation fits his words. Peter's first letter, written to scattered believers, assumes they are being insulted for the name of Christ (1 Peter 4:14-16).
Acts 28:22: "With regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against."
Suetonius (Nero 16) lists punishments on Christians, "a class of men given to a new and harmful superstition".

Futurists expect a worldwide hatred of believers in the final tribulation, beyond the first-century scale. Amillennial readers say "all nations" describes how the church is treated in every age. All agree the early church suffered widely and that Jesus' words gave it courage.
If Matthew 24:9 was fulfilled before AD 70, does that mean Christians today will not face tribulation?
No. Jesus said, "In the world you will have tribulation". The specific prophecy was fulfilled then, but suffering for Christ is part of every age.

The fulfilled reading does not promise an easy life. Jesus said, "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). Paul said that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). He also said all who desire to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). The point is narrower. The specific sufferings in Matthew 24:9 were linked to the time before Jerusalem's fall. Believers today still suffer, and in some lands very severely. But they should not read their troubles as a countdown clock. They can take comfort from how God kept his word to the first church. The same God will strengthen the church now (Romans 8:35-37).
Paul wrote that the folly of false teachers "will be plain to all" (2 Timothy 3:9); God vindicated his church then and can do so now.
Romans 5:3: "We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance."

All Christian views agree that believers suffer in this age. Pretribulationists add that the church will be removed before a future seven-year tribulation of God's wrath. Posttribulationists say the church will go through a final tribulation. Amillennialists see tribulation as the normal mark of the whole age.
Was there a falling away and betrayal among believers before AD 70?
Yes. Paul names people who deserted him, and the letters warn often of false teachers. Jesus said many would fall away and betray one another.

Jesus said many would fall away, betray one another and hate one another (Matthew 24:10). Paul wrote that "all who are in Asia turned away from me", naming Phygelus and Hermogenes (2 Timothy 1:15). Demas left him, "in love with this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). At his first defense "all deserted me" (2 Timothy 4:16). Alexander the coppersmith did him great harm (2 Timothy 4:14). Hymenaeus and Philetus swerved from the truth, saying the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Hebrews warns readers not to drift back from Christ under pressure (Hebrews 6:4-6; 10:26-29). Tacitus says some arrested Christians under Nero gave the names of others (Annals 15.44). On the fulfilled reading, these betrayals fit Jesus' words in the same generation.
Tacitus, Annals 15.44: first those who confessed were seized; then, on their information, a vast number more.
Galatians 1:6: Paul was astonished that the Galatians were "so quickly deserting" the gospel.

Futurists expect a great end-time apostasy, often linked with 2 Thessalonians 2:3. Others note that partial preterists also read 2 Thessalonians 2:3 as first-century. Amillennial readers see falling away as a recurring danger for the church in every generation.
Did false prophets and growing lawlessness mark the church's first generation?
Yes. The later New Testament letters are full of warnings about false teachers already present, and John says "many antichrists have come".

Jesus said many false prophets would arise and lead many astray, and because lawlessness would increase, the love of many would grow cold (Matthew 24:11-12). Peter warned that false teachers would arise among believers, just as false prophets arose in Israel (2 Peter 2:1). Jude says such people "have crept in unnoticed" already (Jude 4). John writes that "many false prophets have gone out into the world" (1 John 4:1). He adds, "Many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour" (1 John 2:18). Jesus' letter to Ephesus says they had "abandoned the love you had at first" (Revelation 2:4). On the fulfilled reading, the apostles saw Jesus' words being fulfilled around them, and they read it as a sign that the end of the age was near.
1 John 2:18: John reasons from the presence of many antichrists to "it is the last hour".
Revelation 2:2: Ephesus tested those who called themselves apostles and found them false.

Many readers agree the apostles saw these warnings fulfilled in their day. Futurists add that a greater climax of deception and lawlessness will come before Christ returns. Amillennial readers say "the last hour" covers the whole time from Christ's first coming to his return.
What "end" did Jesus mean in "the one who endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 24:13)?
On this reading, the end of the age that the disciples asked about: the fall of the temple. Those who held firm and obeyed Jesus' warning were kept safe.
